title: Turmeric and Curcumin for Arthritis: What the Evidence Really Shows (UK Guide)
meta_title: Turmeric & Curcumin for Arthritis: Honest Evidence Guide
meta_description: Turmeric and arthritis: the November2026 Cochrane review, low-certainty knee-osteoarthritis results, liver safety and medicine checks.
excerpt: An updated, cautious turmeric evidence summary using Cochrane, NICE, NHS and NCCIH rather than older encouraging supplement claims.
direct_answer: The November2026 Cochrane review found that turmeric supplements may make little or no difference to knee-osteoarthritis pain, function or quality of life. Evidence certainty was low and harms very uncertain. They do not replace prescribed care.
author: Louis Maxwell
keywords: turmeric arthritis evidence, curcumin osteoarthritis, turmeric supplement safety, turmeric warfarin, turmeric methotrexate, turmeric liver
content:
Quick answer: A Cochrane review published in November 2026 found that turmeric supplements may make little or no difference to pain, function or quality of life in knee osteoarthritis compared with placebo. Confidence in those results was low, and harms were very uncertain. This is not evidence that turmeric is equivalent to ibuprofen, repairs cartilage or can replace arthritis medicines.

Proposed editorial rewrite prepared 26 November 2026. This changed edition is awaiting Louis Maxwell's clinical review.

Why this summary is more cautious

Older summaries of small turmeric trials often sounded encouraging. A newer review can reach a different conclusion when it uses different eligibility rules and checks the trustworthiness of the studies. Readers need the current uncertainty, not a promise carried forward from an earlier headline.

The Cochrane review published 19 November 2026 included nine studies involving 1,245 people with knee osteoarthritis. It assessed evidence available to 7 November 2025. Publication date and search cut-off are different: it should not be described as including every trial published in 2026.

What the review found

Compared with placebo, turmeric supplements may produce little or no improvement in knee pain, physical function or quality of life. There may be a small improvement in how often people rated treatment successful. Confidence in these estimates was low.

The review was even less certain about unwanted effects and people leaving a study because of them. That means it cannot provide a strong reassurance of safety. Small, short studies of different products do not settle whether long-term use is safe.

These findings concern knee osteoarthritis. They should not be extended to rheumatoid arthritis, every painful joint or every turmeric preparation. A result described as uncertain must not become a guaranteed benefit in a product recommendation.

Do not read a comparison as equivalence

A trial comparing turmeric with a pain medicine does not automatically establish that the two work equally well. The design, size and reliability of the study matter. This guide therefore makes no claim that turmeric works as well as ibuprofen or causes fewer important harms.

NICE NG226 places information, therapeutic exercise and weight management when appropriate at the centre of osteoarthritis care. Discuss persistent pain with your healthcare team instead of replacing an agreed treatment with a supplement.

Rheumatoid arthritis is a different decision

NICE NG100 recommendations 1.8.8 to 1.8.10 describe the limitations of diet and complementary therapies in rheumatoid arthritis and advise against using them instead of conventional treatment. A supplement must not delay review of swollen joints or uncontrolled symptoms.

This article does not recommend turmeric for rheumatoid arthritis, claim that it prevents damage or provide a dose. Continue prescribed medicines and contact the treatment team if they are not controlling the condition.

Cooking and concentrated extracts are different

Using a spice in a meal is not the same exposure as taking a concentrated extract. A capsule may also contain other ingredients intended to increase absorption. The words natural or high strength are not proof of safety or a reason to combine several products.

The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health warns that liver damage has been reported with some formulations designed to increase curcumin absorption. It also lists digestive side effects and advises discussing herbal products with a clinician when taking medicines.

Safety checks before taking a product

  • Show a pharmacist the full ingredient list, including any black-pepper extract or other added substances.
  • Give a complete medicine and supplement list. Do not assume that taking an ingredient in food establishes the safety of a concentrated capsule with those medicines.
  • If you take methotrexate, the NHS says safety information for many herbal products and supplements is insufficient. Check before adding one.
  • NCCIH says turmeric supplements during pregnancy may be unsafe, and safety information for amounts above food use during breastfeeding is limited. Seek individual advice.
  • Do not stop prescribed treatment, increase the dose or combine products to chase a faster result.

Symptoms to act on

Stop the turmeric or curcumin product and contact a healthcare professional if you develop possible liver symptoms, such as unusual tiredness, nausea, poor appetite, dark urine or yellowing of the skin or eyes. NCCIH advises stopping the product and seeking advice for these symptoms. Do not simply change brands.

Vomiting blood needs medical help. Follow the NHS urgent and emergency advice: call 999 or go to A&E if it occurs with feeling unwell, faintness, confusion, breathing changes, cold clammy skin, tummy pain or black poo. If it has stopped and there were no other symptoms, seek urgent GP or 111 advice. Do not drive yourself to A&E.

A sudden very painful or swollen joint also needs urgent assessment. Joint infection can occur without fever. Contact an urgent GP service or 111 where available, or the local GP out-of-hours service in Northern Ireland.

Questions before spending money

  • What benefit am I expecting, and does current evidence support that expectation?
  • Has someone checked the actual ingredients against my medicines?
  • Would this cost displace food, heating, transport or treatment that I need?
  • Do worsening symptoms need a clinical review instead of another supplement?

Sources and scope

Sources checked 26 November 2026. Cochrane provides the current knee-osteoarthritis review used here. NICE provides condition-management guidance, NHS sources support medicine and urgent-care advice, and NCCIH supplies the cited product-safety information. This is not a personal prescribing recommendation or a complete review of every curcumin study.
